title: Family angry after opening day of Taser death inquest
article: Testimony about a beating in police custody, and a subsequent autopsy left the family of Clay Willey shaken and angry as a coroner's inquest into his death began Monday.

'It's horrible. It's hard to sit through lies,' said Willey's friend Monique Gonyou. 'I think a lot of what the pathologist was saying was put in his mouth by the RCMP. He (Willey) had been clean for the past five months and the one time he slips up is the day he died.'
Pathologist Dr. James McNaughton testified that Willey, 33, died from cocaine use, an overdose or cocaine toxicity in his blood.
The RCMP used a Taser to subdue Willey during his arrest in Prince George in July 2003.
He died a day later.
While Willey had heart and drug problems, his family believes it was the Taser that led to his death.
Pre-inquest speculation pointed a finger at the RCMP's use of physical force to subdue Willey and their use of a Taser stun gun as possible contributors to his death.
But, McNaughton testified, in his estimation, these were not relevant factors.
'The electrical current is what is of concern in the use of Taser guns,' McNaughton said. 'The shocks are brief in nature and the current doesn't linger in the body.
'For there to be a relationship between the shock and the death, the death should occur in a finite period of time, four or five minutes at most, after the application of the shock.'
Willey continued to struggle for several minutes after the application of the shock and did not die until the next morning.
Presiding coroner David Coverdale outlined the arrest for the jury.

When officers attempted to physically obtain compliance, Willey aggressively resisted. Police used physical force, pepper spray and handcuffs to restrain him. As Willey continued to struggle, officers applied a hog-tie restraint before transporting him to the detachment.
Willey continued to struggle while in an RCMP cellblock. At that point, a Taser gun was used to bring him under control.
He was Tasered twice, according to the pathologist. He continued to struggle for a time, then went suddenly docile.

An ambulance was called and by 5:36 p.m. he was en route to hospital. While travelling, Willey went into cardiac arrest but was revived. Emergency Room personnel treated him then moved him to the Intensive Care Unit. He lived through the night, but was pronounced dead at 9:05 a.m. on July 22.

Coupled with a toxicology report that found the presence of cocaine in Willey's system and indications of heart damage consistent with prolonged drug use, McNaughton determined the death was as a result of a condition known as cocaine psychosis or agitated delirium.
Willey's mother was upset by comments from McNaughton during cross- examination by the family's lawyer, Dan Weatherly.
Weatherly asked how one of Willey's molars could have come to have gone missing.

McNaughton confirmed teeth were missing, including the molar, but he was unable to determine when it might have been dislodged. There was no corresponding facial injury to indicate the tooth was lost during the fight with police, he said.
Willey's mother, Gloria, however, said the testimony as at odds with what they had been told at the hospital after the man died.
'The nurse at the hospital told us the bleeding in his mouth was from the teeth they knocked out,' said Willey's mother Gloria.
Willey's girlfriend Miranda Savard, was also critical of police.
'It has taken us a long time to get this inquest to happen, and, hopefully, the truth will come out,' she said.
Willey's sister Bryna, too, points a finger of blame at the RCMP.
'There were times Clayton had been told by the police that they were going to get him. Going to kill him,' Bryna said.
'He feared the police. He paid people to walk with him to feel safer. He died in the way he most feared.'
The Prince George RCMP has said it will observe the process and implement any recommendations the investigation produces.

'It is a fact-finding process that allows for a full disclosure of the facts. We welcome the opportunity to describe our actions, as pertains to this particular case,' said RCMP media communications officer Const. Gary Godwin.

'The inquest is a forum that allows us to disclose our investigative steps, finding for the ultimate goal of ensuring that we are providing the best possible police services to the communities we police,' Godwin said.
The inquest is scheduled for two weeks.
